logline: A brilliant, unknowable ad man at a 1960s Manhattan agency keeps reinventing himself as the world around him shifts - and the cost of that reinvention is everything he loves.

renewal.note: Series concluded May 17, 2015 after seven seasons and 92 episodes on AMC.

bollymeter.basis: Season 1 won the Emmy for Outstanding Drama Series on its very first submission - a basic cable first. Critics were unanimous that Matthew Weiner had engineered something formally new: a prestige drama that was also a period excavation and a character study of impossible density.

pull_quotes.text: Mad Men is nothing short of a masterpiece.

seasons.review_body: Mad Men Season 1 arrives fully formed - a period drama set in a 1960 Sterling Cooper ad agency that is, beneath its immaculate surface, a forensic study of American masculinity in crisis. Don Draper, played with reptilian charisma by Jon Hamm, is the show's engine: a man whose identity is entirely constructed, whose genius is selling other people their own fantasies. Critics in 2007 were stunned by the show's confidence - the long silences, the refusal to explain, the way it trusted viewers to sit with unease. The debut season won AMC its first Emmy for Outstanding Drama Series, making history as the first basic cable winner. Beneath the period detail - cigarette smoke, martinis, sexism worn as cologne - the show is asking what it costs a person to be completely unknowable.

episode_reviews.title: Smoke Gets in Your Eyes
episode_reviews.spoiler_free: The pilot establishes Don Draper's world in a single bravura sequence: the Lucky Strike pitch. It also introduces Peggy Olson on her first day, and the contrast - the man at the top of his constructed self, the woman just beginning to find hers - is the architecture of the entire series. Visually meticulous, the pilot is cold, seductive, and immediately unlike anything else on TV.
episode_reviews.the_moment: Don's cigarette pitch reframe at the Lucky Strike meeting - the show announcing exactly what kind of intelligence it operates with.

critic_note.text: A pilot of extraordinary poise and formal control, introducing a world instantly, utterly its own.

bollymeter.basis: Critics consider Season 2 the point where the show's historical canvas expanded - the Cuban Missile Crisis, the early stirrings of the 1960s social rupture - without sacrificing the intimate scale that made Season 1 work.

seasons.review_body: Season 2 expands the world outward. The Cuban Missile Crisis arrives as an existential backdrop, and Weiner uses it to stress-test every character-what do you do when the world might end? Don's backstory deepens, Peggy's arc takes a decisive turn, and Joan begins to show the fractures beneath her armored competence. The second season operates with the confidence of a story that has already established its core premises, turning its setup into forward momentum and treating its own institutional identity as a narrative engine.
seasons.season_over_season: Season 2 broadens the historical frame while deepening every major character - a textbook strong sophomore run.

bollymeter.basis: Season 3 ends with one of the show's boldest structural moves - the dissolution and reformation of Sterling Cooper - which critics read as Weiner blowing up his own setup to prevent stagnation.

seasons.review_body: Season 3 builds methodically through the Kennedy assassination and concludes with a structural coup: Don dismantles and rebuilds the agency in a single finale. The season commits to historical specificity, and the JFK assassination episode is moving without turning exploitative. The finale, "Shut the Door. Have a Seat," functions like a heist movie condensed into a drama finale.
seasons.season_over_season: Season 3 uses historical events more explicitly than its predecessors and rewards patience with a finale that resets the board entirely.

bollymeter.basis: Critics frequently identify Season 4 as the show's creative peak - Don at his most stripped down, the new SCDP agency as a blank canvas, and the writing at its most economical.

seasons.review_body: Season 4 stands as Mad Men's apex. Don is alone, newly divorced, living in a bare apartment, and the show uses that emptiness as a mirror. The writing sharpens into something ruthless. "The Suitcase" (Ep 7) becomes an almost two-hander between Don and Peggy, built around the friction of their private truths colliding with professional roles. The season wins its fourth consecutive Emmy for Outstanding Drama Series. The stripped-down character focus functions as the show's clearest expression of its core themes and machinery.
seasons.season_over_season: Season 4 strips away the institutional comfort of the established agency and uses Don's exposure to achieve the series' most sustained emotional intensity.

bollymeter.basis: Season 5 introduced Megan as Don's new wife and the mid-1960s cultural upheaval as a full-bore narrative force. Critics were mostly enthusiastic; some felt the show's glacial pace was starting to strain.

seasons.review_body: Season 5 returns after an eighteen-month hiatus with Don remarried and the 1960s counterculture arriving at the SCDP door. Megan is a disruptive addition, and her placement reorganizes the season’s interpersonal dynamics, pushing plotlines into sharper, less predictable territory. The Lane Pryce storyline delivers the season’s emotional gut-punch, executed with the show’s characteristic restraint. The season opener - a three-minute sequence set to “A Little Less Conversation” - signals immediately that Weiner is escalating rather than coasting.
seasons.season_over_season: Season 5 trades the intimate focus of Season 4 for a wider social canvas; gains in scope, slight loss in emotional precision.

bollymeter.basis: Critics were divided on Season 6 - Don's darker, more self-destructive turn read to some as repetition; others saw it as the show's most explicit engagement with the late 1960s as an empire cracking at the foundation.

seasons.review_body: Season 6 is constructed to fracture its own momentum. Don cheats again, self-sabotages again, and the season repeatedly questions whether the audience's patience with a man constitutionally incapable of change becomes a form of complicity. The Vietnam backdrop and the 1968 setting give the story its most explicitly political texture. The Crash (Ep 8) works as a deliberately disorienting experiment, while In Care Of (the finale) lands with sustained harrow. The season can feel repetitive, and that repetition reads less like accident than like a test of whether the recurring pattern carries meaning.
seasons.season_over_season: Season 6 risks feeling circular; it earns that circularity in the finale but the journey taxes patience more than any prior season.

bollymeter.basis: The split final season (aired across 2014-2015) delivered a finale that critics debated furiously - the Coca-Cola coda either the show's ultimate cynical joke or its most optimistic frame, depending on who you ask.

seasons.review_body: The final season delivers endings for Peggy, Joan, Roger, and Don with a sense of closure that feels carefully engineered rather than rushed. Peggy's arc - from secretary to creative director - stands as the show's most satisfying long game. The 'Person to Person' finale is built around Don's spiritual collapse and the possibility of rebirth in an Esalen retreat, then closes on a Coca-Cola ad that reframes his identity in one of prestige TV's most loaded final images. The meaning of that ad stays contested, and the story sustains that uncertainty instead of resolving it into a single moral verdict, which becomes the point of the finale.
seasons.season_over_season: The final season resolves the series' core threads with more grace than Season 6 suggested was possible - Peggy's closing scene alone justifies the entire run.
